content_html:
Predictive Processing & Free-Energy Principle

Memory lives inside a hierarchical generative model that aims to minimize surprise (variational free energy). Perception, learning, action, and memory are different modes of the same prediction machinery.

Perception ≈ infer latent causes that best predict sensations (prediction-error minimization).
Learning ≈ update model parameters/priors so future prediction errors shrink (free-energy minimization over time).
Action (active inference) ≈ sample the world so sensations match predictions or reduce uncertainty.
Memory ≈ the model’s parameters, precision estimates, and cached trajectories (episodic traces/replay) used to predict and plan.

Mathematical core

Given observations x, latent causes z, and model p(x,z), the brain maintains an approximate posterior q(z) and minimizes the variational free energy F = E_q[\ln q(z) - \ln p(x,z)], which upper-bounds surprise -\ln p(x). Gradients on F yield predictive-coding style updates: descending prediction errors weighted by precision (the inverse of uncertainty).

Where memory sits in the loop

Parameters & priors: long-term semantic structure that shapes top-down predictions.
Precision weights: attention-like control that selects (weights) errors worth learning from.
Episodic traces & replay: cached trajectories the system replays to plan and consolidate (hippocampal replay/predictive maps).

On this view, remembering is controlled imagination: running the generative model with constraints from cues to explain the present or simulate the future.

Select – Change – Reconstruct

Select → precision-weighted attention picks which errors to heed (and which memories to access).
Change → learning updates parameters/priors to reduce free energy across contexts.
Reconstruct → generative replay & scene construction recombine memory fragments to predict/plan.
